pages.name: Stress
pages.text: A thicker bar spreads the same pull over more metal. So divide the force by the area of the bar's section. That is the [[stress]], in newtons per square millimetre. A 20 mm bar has 314 mm² of section. A 10 kN pull on it gives 31.8 N/mm². A 10 mm bar has a quarter of that area. The same 10 kN on it gives four times the stress, 127 N/mm². Stress is not a force.

pages.name: Work out a stress
pages.task: A rod has 40 mm² of section. It carries a 6 kN pull. What is the stress in it?
pages.why: Put the force in newtons first. 6 kN is 6000 N. Then share it over the section: 6000 ÷ 40 = 150. So each square millimetre carries 150 N. The stress is 150 N/mm².

pages.name: Shear
pages.text: A pull acts along a bar. A [[shear]] load acts across a part instead. It tries to slide one side of a cut past the other. This pin joins two plates pulled opposite ways. The pin is cut across where the plates meet. Its [[shear stress]] is the force ÷ the area of that cut. A 10 mm pin has 78.5 mm² of section. A 5 kN load across it gives 63.7 N/mm².

pages.name: A key cut across
pages.task: A key locks a pulley to its shaft. It is cut across over 8 mm by 40 mm. It carries a 16 kN shear load. What is the shear stress in it?
pages.why: The cut is 8 × 40 = 320 mm². The load is 16 000 N. Share it over the cut: 16 000 ÷ 320 = 50. So the shear stress is 50 N/mm².

pages.name: Strain
pages.text: A longer bar stretches further under the same stress, because every millimetre of it stretches the same. So divide the stretch by the length. That is the [[strain]]. It is a length over a length, so it has no units. These two steel bars carry the same stress. The 1 m bar stretches 0.5 mm and the 2 m bar 1 mm. Both have a strain of 0.0005, or 0.05%.

pages.name: The tensile test
pages.text: A tensile test pulls a bar steadily and records the force and the stretch. This steel bar has 100 mm² of section and marks 100 mm apart. At low stress, strain rises in step with stress. So the curve starts straight. Its slope is stress ÷ strain, called Young's modulus. It is the metal's stiffness. Steel's is about 200 000 N/mm². At 20 kN the bar reads 200 N/mm² and 0.1%, a 0.1 mm stretch. With the load off, it springs back to its first length.

pages.name: Find a stiffness
pages.task: An aluminium alloy bar reads 70 N/mm² at 0.1% strain, on its straight start. What is its Young's modulus?
pages.why: Young's modulus is stress ÷ strain. Turn the per cent into a fraction first. 0.1% is 0.001. Then 70 ÷ 0.001 = 70 000 N/mm². That is about a third of steel's. So the same stress stretches it about three times as far.

pages.name: Past yield
pages.text: Past its [[yield strength]], the bar starts to stretch for good. This steel's is 250 N/mm². Take the load off then, and only part of the stretch springs back. It comes back along a line parallel to the straight start. The bar keeps the rest. Many metals bend over with no clear corner, like the faint curve. Their yield strength is usually taken where the dashed line cuts the curve. That line starts at 0.2% strain and runs parallel to the straight start.

pages.task: This bar is let go at 10 mm of stretch, at 360 N/mm². How much stretch does it keep?

pages.name: Peak, neck and break
pages.text: Pull on and the stress climbs to a peak. That peak is the [[tensile strength]]. This steel's is 400 N/mm². Past it, the bar thins at one spot into a neck. The neck loses area faster than the metal gets stronger, so the force falls until it breaks. Stiffness is the slope of the straight start. Strength is the height of the peak. A metal can be stiff and weak, or springy and strong.

pages.name: Ductile or brittle
pages.text: Mild steel is [[ductile]]. It stretches a long way and necks before it breaks. A [[brittle]] material, such as glass or a ceramic, breaks with hardly any permanent stretch. [[Toughness]] is the energy a material soaks up before it breaks. It is the area under its curve. So a ductile metal is usually the tougher one. [[Hardness]] is different again. It is how well a surface resists denting or scratching.

pages.task: Bar A is brittle, and its curve has the steeper straight start. Bar B is ductile, with the higher peak. Which bar is stiffer?
pages.why: Stiffness is the slope of the straight start. A's is steeper, so the same stress stretches A less. B's higher peak makes B stronger, and its larger area makes it tougher. Neither makes it stiffer.

pages.name: Safety
pages.text: A part is designed to run well below its yield strength. The [[factor of safety]] is the failing stress ÷ the working stress. At a working stress of 100 N/mm², this steel has a factor of 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5 on yield. The [[safe working load]] is the working stress × the area of the section. For the 100 mm² test bar, that is 100 × 100 = 10 000 N, or 10 kN.

pages.name: Fatigue
pages.text: Even well below yield, a load that comes and goes can crack a part. At a flaw or a sharp corner, such as a keyway, the stress is higher than in the rest. A crack starts there and grows a little with each cycle, until the part breaks. That is [[fatigue]]. A shaft bends a little under its load. As it turns, every spot on its surface feels this.

pages.name: A safe working load
pages.task: A 20 mm steel bar yields at 250 N/mm². It needs a factor of safety of 5 on yield. What is its safe working load?
pages.why: The working stress is 250 ÷ 5 = 50 N/mm². The bar's area is π × 10² = 314 mm². So the load is 50 × 314 = 15 700 N, or 15.7 kN.

pages.task: A 3 m steel tie has 200 mm² of section. It carries 20 kN. How far does it stretch?
pages.why: The stress is 20 000 ÷ 200 = 100 N/mm². The strain is 100 ÷ 200 000 = 0.0005. The tie is 3000 mm long. So it stretches 0.0005 × 3000 = 1.5 mm.
